summary:
I read the whole stack: the kept-gesture module (Kotlin GestureRecognizer in IMAGE mode, Gemma via LiteRT-LM, pinned model downloads, verdict.ts tested in Jest), keeper.ts, proofVerify.ts, v4.ts (/api/proof/challenge, /api/proof/habit), habits.ts, rules.ts (the challenge lasts 2 min plus 60 s grace and the gestures are Thumb_Up, Victory and Open_Palm), the Prisma models, Proof.tsx, features/objects, the http ProofApi and the Keeper voice/sfx code. I edited nothing and ran no builds.

Four things already in the repo shape the design:
- The ElevenLabs count clips are already generated: frontend/assets/voice/count-1..50.mp3 plus go, done, half-rep ("That wasn't a rep. Go lower."), lost and freeze ("Freeze! Thumbs up. Now."), made by backend/scripts/keeper_count_voice.ts.
- The catalog already has a `push_ups` entry, set to object:null.
- OBJECT_TEXT_RE already accepts "20 push-ups".
- The program's object_id is only a tag now (habits.ts).

So a Rep Oath fits with almost no data-model change. A habit's object text is "20 push-ups" or "30 squats", and a parser turns it into an exercise and a target. Creation, the per-habit challenge, /proof/verify → /api/proof/habit, the receipt, combinedHabitsHash and record_checkin all stay as they are.

The counter is a pure TypeScript module, packages/engine/src/reps.ts, with no dependencies:
- **Angles:** aspect-corrected 2D joint angles.
- **Side choice:** it uses the side whose weakest needed joint is most visible, and only switches when the other side is better by 0.15.
- **Smoothing:** an EMA that accounts for the time between frames (τ = 60 ms), with rejection of single-frame landmark flips.
- **State machine with hysteresis:** setup → up → descending → down → up. It also has lost and paused states.
- **Thresholds:**
  - Push-up: elbow angle starts a rep below 130°, counts as down below 90°, up above 160°. Body line (shoulder-hip-ankle) at least 150°. The shoulder-to-ankle line within 35° of horizontal, which blocks standing elbow-bends. Knee angle at least 140°. Shoulders not facing the camera. Rep length 0.6–8 s.
  - Squat: knee angle starts a rep below 140°, down below 100°, up above 160°. Hip no more than 0.15 thigh-lengths above the knee at the bottom. Torso at least 30° from horizontal at the bottom and at least 65° when standing. Rep length 0.8–10 s.
- **Events:** half reps, no-lockout bounces, too fast, too slow and form faults all produce events. A form fault on more than 25% of a rep's frames rejects that rep.

The phone feeds the counter the same quantised 20 Hz samples it puts in the trace. Running `countReps(decodeTrace(trace))` therefore gives the live count exactly, on the phone and on the server.

The evidence sent is:
- the quantised trace: 12 joints × (x, y, visibility) at up to 20 Hz, with timestamps and the pause window;
- the phone's rep timestamps;
- three keyframes taken from the analysis frames at exact sample times: the bottom of a random rep in the first half, the top of a random rep in the second half, and the bottom of the last rep;
- the freeze frame, sent as the existing `photo` field. The freeze gesture is the challenge's gesture, which comes from the blockhash.

The server, the Keeper:
1. recounts the trace with the same function;
2. runs hard checks that cost nothing: duration within the challenge window, frame gaps, one freeze pause of 2–8 s between two reps, and keyframe angles matching their claimed phase;
3. records soft flags: reps too evenly timed, and bone lengths that vary too much;
4. only then makes one multi-image vision call. It asks whether each frame shows a real person in the claimed phase, whether any frame looks like a screen, whether it is the same person and scene throughout, and whether the freeze frame shows the challenge gesture. The answer maps onto the existing PhotoVerdict and verdictPasses.

The receipt gets an optional `reps` block: exercise, target, server repCount, traceSha256, keyframe hashes, freeze rep and gesture, tempo, and flags. canonicalJson drops undefined fields, so photo receipts hash exactly as before.

What is still spoofable:
- A patched client can upload a made-up trace together with real, recompressed photos.
- Video played on a screen is caught only by the vision model.
- Nothing ties the set to a particular person.

It is still much stronger than one photo. A single photo shows someone held an object for a second. This shows a continuous, physically consistent skeleton doing N reps inside a fresh window, with four images that agree with it, one of them showing a gesture fixed by the blockhash at a moment the user could not plan for.

Two blockers need the backend. First, the 2-minute challenge (+60 s grace) is too short for 50 reps, so rep habits need a longer upload grace. Second, the /proof/verify rep branch has to be added. CLAUDE.md makes backend/ read-only for frontend work outside merge phase, so both go into docs/BACKEND_GAPS.md unless the user approves backend edits.
decisions: Rep Oath data model: habitObjects[i] = "<target> push-ups" | "<target> squats" (lower case, matches OBJECT_TEXT_RE). parseRepHabit() in the shared module is the only way to detect a rep habit, on the phone and the server. The target is 1–50, because count clips exist for 1–50 and the set must fit the challenge window. No Prisma, program or route-shape changes are needed for creation. The on-chain object_id stays a tag. The goal hash already covers the habit text.

Creation (C2): add catalog entries for push-ups and squats (the existing `push_ups` entry, plus a new `squats` entry) with a `reps` exercise field. Choosing one opens a target stepper (10/20/30/50) and writes repHabitText(exercise, target) as both the habit name and the habit object. objectNameOfText and objectIconOfText get a rep special case ("20 push-ups", icon arm-flex).

Proof flow: no new route. Shoot (F1) renders a <RepSet> instead of the photo camera when parseRepHabit(h.object) is not null. The challenge comes from the same POST /api/proof/challenge {habit} call, fetched when the user taps Start, so its gesture is known before the set and becomes the freeze gesture. On finish, it stores image = the freeze JPEG plus the rep evidence in useProof and goes to F2 Check. ProofApi.submit gains an optional `reps` argument, and http sends it inside the same /proof/verify body. The pass, fail, unavailable and expired screens and /api/proof/habit are unchanged. The Demo mock accepts the evidence and passes when countReps(trace) >= target.

Counting runs in JS on the native module's pose samples, not in Kotlin. That keeps one TypeScript implementation that the phone and the server share (packages/engine/src/reps.ts, tested with tsx --test, and imported in the app as @kept/engine). The backend gets a byte-identical copy at backend/src/shared/reps.ts, following the payout.ts precedent, plus a test that checks the two files have the same SHA-256.

Determinism: the native side emits at most 20 Hz. RepSession quantises each sample to integers (x and y × 1000, visibility × 100) before feeding the counter, and stores exactly those integers in the trace. Pause and resume take effect at the next sample boundary and are recorded as windows. The live count therefore equals countReps(decodeTrace(trace)), on the phone before sending and on the server.

Angles use 2D image coordinates corrected for aspect ratio (x × width/height), not worldLandmarks. 2D is reliable side-on and is what the trace can carry cheaply. Setup copy asks for a side view: phone landscape on the floor about 2 m away for push-ups; portrait, side-on or at 45°, for squats.

Side selection: the score of a side is the visibility of its weakest needed joint, set to 0 if that joint is out of frame. It switches sides only when the other side is better by 0.15, and resets the EMA when it switches. A frame is unusable below visibility 0.5. 400 ms without a usable frame means lost: the rep in progress is dropped, and a start pose held for 500 ms is needed again.

Smoothing: an EMA that uses the time between samples, α = 1 − exp(−dt/60 ms), which gives α ≈ 0.57 at 20 Hz. A jump of more than 60° from the smoothed value is treated as a landmark flip and dropped, up to 2 frames in a row. The 70° gap between the down and up thresholds is the main protection against jitter.

Push-up rules: a rep starts when the elbow angle drops below 130°, the bottom is below 90°, and the rep counts when the angle rises above 160°. Rep length 600 ms–8 s. Faults: turn_side (shoulders more than 0.6 torso-lengths apart horizontally in the image), not_plank (shoulder-to-ankle line more than 35° from horizontal, which kills standing elbow-bends), hips (shoulder-hip-ankle angle under 150°), knees (knee angle under 140°). The start pose is elbow above 160°, plank-like and side-on, held for 500 ms.

Squat rules: a rep starts when the knee angle drops below 140°, the bottom is below 100°, and the rep counts above 160°. Rep length 800 ms–10 s. Faults: lean (hip-to-shoulder line under 30° from horizontal, which also catches someone lying down and bending their knees), depth (at the deepest frame the hip is more than 0.15 thigh-lengths above the knee). The start pose is knee above 160° and torso at least 65° from horizontal.

Rep outcomes: a rep that never reaches the bottom gives half_rep (the Keeper says "That wasn't a rep. Go lower.", at most once every 8 s). A second dip without locking out gives rejected:no_lockout. Under the minimum length gives too_fast. Over the maximum gives too_slow and goes back to setup. Any one fault on more than 25% of a rep's frames, or a depth fault at the bottom, gives rejected:<fault>. The fault event fires when a fault starts, so the UI can show a hint chip.

Live UX: full-screen preview with the skeleton drawn natively (no 30 Hz React renders). A large Geist Mono counter "12" with "/ 20" under it and a progress ring. A depth gauge driven by a Reanimated shared value set from counter.angle on each sample. One form-hint chip, a challenge timer chip, and an Abort button. Phases: framing guide → 'ready' → the 'go' clip → counting (count-N clip plus a light haptic per rep) → freeze → counting → stop automatically at the target with the 'done' clip → F2. Any 'lost' event plays the 'lost' clip, at most once every 5 s. Voice respects useSettings.keeperVoice. All strings are new additions.reps.* copy keys.

Voice playback: expo-audio with 3 players in rotation. After rep n it preloads count-(n+1) and count-(n+2). If a clip is still playing when the next rep lands, the newer number replaces it. Metro needs static require() calls, so assets/voice/index.ts lists all 55 requires (generate it).

Freeze liveness: k is a random rep, using a secure random source on the phone, between ceil(0.3·target) and ceil(0.7·target), with a floor of 1. After rep k at the top: requestPause, play 'freeze-<gesture>' and show a large gesture overlay. At +1.5 s the native side returns the analysis frame at the latest sample time, and that becomes the `photo`. At +3.5 s requestResume, and counting continues once a start pose is held for 500 ms. The freeze gesture is the challenge gesture (blockhash-derived), so the existing expectedGesture check in /proof/verify applies unchanged. That needs two new clips, freeze-victory and freeze-open-palm, added to keeper_count_voice.ts LINES; only the thumbs-up clip exists today.

Keyframes: three plus the freeze frame. The bottom of a random rep in [2, floor(target/2)], the top of a random rep in the second half, and the bottom of the final rep. Native keeps a ring buffer of about 1 s of downscaled analysis frames keyed by sample timestamp. keyframe(tAbs) returns a 512 px JPEG (quality 80, about 40–70 KB) as base64 plus its sha256. Each image therefore corresponds exactly to a trace sample.

Evidence payload (body.reps of /proof/verify): { trace: {v:1, engine:'reps@1', exercise, aspect, t:int[], p:int[] (36 per sample), pauses:[[a,b]]}, reps:[{startT,bottomT,endT}], freeze:{afterRep, promptT, t}, keyframes:[{kind:'bottom'|'top', rep, t, jpeg}] }. photo = the freeze JPEG. A set is at most 240 s, so at most 4,800 samples and about 0.7 MB of JSON; a typical set is 150–400 KB, well under express.json's 12 MB limit.

Server (rep branch of /proof/verify, chosen when parseRepHabit(expectedObject) is not null): (1) validate and decode the trace; (2) countReps must be >= target; (3) hard plausibility checks: duration ≤ min(240 s, now − challenge.issuedAt), largest sample gap ≤ 1 s, exactly one pause of 2–8 s placed between rep k and rep k+1, freeze t inside the pause, each keyframe t is a trace sample whose raw angle fits its kind within 15°; (4) soft flags kept in the receipt: rep-length coefficient of variation under 0.04, upper-arm or thigh length varying more than 30%; (5) only when (1)–(3) pass, one multi-image vision call; (6) build the verdict, receipt.reps, receiptHash and the rest of the existing flow. A trace that fails a hard check fails without a paid model call.

Receipt: add an optional `reps` field (left undefined for photo receipts, so their hashes don't change). It holds { engine, exercise, target, repCount (server), phoneCount, durationMs, traceSha256 = sha256(canonicalJson(trace)), keyframes:[{kind,t,sha256}], freeze:{afterRep,gesture,t}, tempo:{medianMs,minMs}, flags:[] }. photoSha256 = the freeze frame, so the existing rule that an identical photo passes only once still applies. habitProof.proofHash = receiptHash, which goes on chain unchanged.

Challenge window for rep habits: the server must use CHALLENGE_UPLOAD_GRACE_MS + REP_SET_MAX_MS (240 s) in currentChallenge, both in /proof/verify and in /api/proof/habit; in /proof/habit, compute texts[h] before looking up the challenge. The phone fetches the challenge when the user taps Start. This is a backend change and goes in docs/BACKEND_GAPS.md. Until it lands, Live can only support sets that finish in about 2.5 minutes.

Scope: per CLAUDE.md, backend/ is read-only for frontend work unless the user says 'merge phase' or 'you may edit the backend'. The shared module, the app, the mock and the native module are frontend work. The /proof/verify rep branch, the challenge grace, Receipt.reps, the multi-image judge and storing keyframe dHashes go in docs/BACKEND_GAPS.md with the request and response shapes above, unless the user approves backend edits. The user did say they have repo access to push.
risks: The backend blocks Live today. The challenge lasts CHALLENGE_TTL_MS (2 min) plus CHALLENGE_UPLOAD_GRACE_MS (60 s), and both /proof/verify and /api/proof/habit reject anything later. Even 20 slow push-ups plus setup and the freeze can run past that. Rep habits need a longer grace, and /proof/verify needs the rep branch. Both are backend changes, which CLAUDE.md does not allow outside merge phase, so the user has to approve them or they go in docs/BACKEND_GAPS.md.

What can still be faked: a patched app or a direct API call can upload a made-up trace. It could replay a real set recorded once, with added jitter, since landmark traces are easy to script. It could pair that with old keyframes re-encoded so the exact-hash duplicate check misses them, plus a new 5-second freeze photo with the right gesture. That is the strongest attack. It costs some effort but is not hard. Ways to reduce it later: store perceptual hashes of keyframes per wallet and reject near-duplicates across days, Play Integrity attestation, and raising the server's evidence bar over time. Why this is still much stronger than one photo: the freeze gesture is fixed by the blockhash and has to appear at a random rep, the set has to fit the challenge window, the skeleton has to be physically consistent, the images have to match the trace, and the same person has to appear in all four images.

Filming a screen playing a video: MediaPipe will happily track a person on a screen. Only the vision model's looksLikeScreenOrPrintout check on four frames stops it, together with the need to hit the right gesture at the moment the phone asks for it.

Camera angle tricks: a 2D elbow angle depends on perspective. Flaring the elbows toward the camera can make a shallow rep look deeper. The turn_side check, the not_plank incline check and the vision model's bottom-phase check on keyframes reduce this but don't remove it. Squats filmed from the front give unreliable knee angles, so the setup copy must ask for a side or 45° view.

Visibility values in MediaPipe tasks-vision 0.10.35 on Android: NormalizedLandmark.visibility() returns an Optional. Check on a real device that it is filled in LIVE_STREAM mode. If it isn't, the native side should send presence() or 1.0 for joints inside the frame, and VIS_MIN may need tuning.

Different JS engines: the phone runs Hermes and the server runs Node V8. Math.acos, atan2 and exp can differ in the last bit, so a rep sitting exactly on a threshold could in theory count differently. The risk is negligible, but the server should accept repCount >= target, and the receipt keeps both phoneCount and repCount for any dispute.

False rejections hurt more here than with photos: someone who just did 50 push-ups and fails is far angrier than someone retaking a photo. Keep the vision rule lenient on phase (at least n−1 frames) and strict on screens, people and the gesture. Never fail a set on a soft flag alone. Tune the thresholds (160° lockout, 150° body line) on real people before launch; 155° may be needed for lockout.

Performance: Pose Landmarker lite or full, preview, a ring buffer of keyframes and 20 Hz events into JS all run together on the phone. The skeleton must be drawn natively; React renders only on rep or hint events, and the depth gauge goes through a Reanimated shared value. A 1 s ring buffer of 512 px bitmaps is about 15–20 MB. Encoding each frame to JPEG as it arrives is cheaper on memory.

Holding a one-handed thumbs-up in a plank at rep k is hard for beginners. If testing shows it is too hard, do the push-up freeze in the kneeling or standing position after a pause. The plausibility check's freeze timing rule still applies.

Voice gaps: only 'Freeze! Thumbs up. Now.' exists. Two more clips are needed, freeze-victory and freeze-open-palm, because the challenge gesture can be Victory or Open_Palm. The generator script is in backend/scripts. Copy keys additions.reps.* must be added to frontend/src/copy/additions.json, since the rule is no hardcoded strings.

The vision call gets more expensive: one call with four images instead of one. The default model, google/gemma-3-27b-it, accepts several images, but the larger request may need a longer VISION_TIMEOUT_MS. It still counts as one check toward DAILY_PHOTO_CHECKS.
